It was not on a whim.
I was sitting in gridlock when I made the decision.
While I was mulling it over, my husband found the house.
It was raining and the bus never came.
In March I packed up the apartment and took the plunge.
You said you moved out of Sao Paulo. Was that a sudden thing?
Not at all. I was mulling it over for two years while everybody thought I was joking.
What was the last straw, then?
There was no single one. I was sitting in gridlock one Tuesday and I just snapped. Quietly.
I know that feeling. I did the same thing in 2016, and three people tried to talk me out of it.
Two tried with me. They said I was being restless.
And were you?
For two years, yes. Then in March I packed up the apartment and took the plunge. It was daunting for about a week.
I was living in Sao Paulo and spending three hours a day in traffic.
One Tuesday I was sitting in gridlock and I just snapped.
It was not on a whim. I mulled it over for two years.

I had a very ordinary job in London and a very ordinary apartment, and for about four years I told everybody I was perfectly happy. Then one Tuesday in February I was standing on the platform at half past six, in the rain, and the train was cancelled for the third time that week. I was not angry. That is the part nobody believes. I was completely calm, and I heard myself say out loud, I am not doing this again. Two women turned and looked at me. I went home, I told my wife, and she said she had waited eleven years for me to say it. We spent that spring mulling it over, and in September we packed up the apartment. People still ask me what the last straw was. It was not the train. The train was simply the morning I finally heard myself.

The first time I wanted to leave Frankfurt I was twenty-nine, and two people talked me out of it in one single afternoon. They were being kind. They said I was restless, that everybody feels like that at twenty-nine, and that in a year I would laugh about it. They were wrong, but I believed them, and I stayed for nine more years. The second time I did not ask anybody. I was driving home on a Friday, the traffic was not moving, and I was listening to the same radio show I had listened to every Friday for nine years. I did not snap. I simply understood something. On Monday I started looking at houses, and I did not tell one single person until the contract was signed. It was not a whim. It was nine years of thinking and one Friday of deciding.
